power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An analyst with complete data reports the species difference. We treat that as the benchmark, impose MAR missingness on sepal width (logit P = a + 0.7•z(sepal length)) 2000 times, and re-estimate with the same procedure. π method mean ζ κ share of intervals containing ζ full still detected 0.20 Listwise 0.434 0.062 0.999 0.44 0.20 MI-pooled 0.266 0.425 0.967 0.06 0.20 MI-group-wise 0.425 0.081 0.996 0.40 0.40 Listwise 0.399 0.136 0.986 0.24 0.40 MI-pooled 0.069 0.850 0.741 0.00 0.40 MI-group-wise 0.388 0.160 0.985 0.22 With 40% of sepal-width values missing, the default imputation model returns ζ = 0.07 against a complete-data 0.46 and detects the species difference in none of 2000 replications. Group-wise imputation detects it as often as listwise deletion does. The pooled model does more than cost power. It removes the effect.

Coverage falls as the sample grows (Figure2, lower row). At 40% missing it goes from 0.992 at N = 40 to 0.703 at N = 320: a nominal 95% interval covers the truth barely seven times in ten, and the larger study is the one misled. In the figure only the pooled arm leaves the nominal line, and it does not return to it. The mechanism is arithmetic rather than subtle -the bias is fixed while the interval narrows at rate 1/√N, so the ratio of bias to standard error grows without bound. That inversion is the point: more data makes the inference worse, and nothing signals it, because the pooled arm's intervals are if anything wider than nominal at small N (0.992 coverage at N = 40 looks reassuring). The robustness design reproduces the collapse more strongly: coverage 0.984 → 0.584 (π = 0.40, N = 40 → 320), and 0.989 → 0.862 at π = 0.20. Power. The same distortion costs detections. At π = 0.40, N = 320 the pooled arm rejects ζ = 0 in 0.482 of replications against group-wise imputation's 0.897 -the default imputation model halves the power to find a real difference (results/sequel_grid.csv, power).3. The attenuation is a law, and we can write it downSources: §Theory; R/verify_conj011. R; R/drv004_closedform.R; results/sequel_kappa_curve_cf.csv. Because missingness depends on Y alone, E[X | Y, observed] = ρ g •Y survives selection. Writing A = P(R = 1)•E[Y² | R = 1] for the observed-case share of the second moment and B = P(R = 0)•E[Y² | R = 0] for the missing-case share, the completed within-group covariance is a blend Cov g (X*, Y) = ρ g •A + b•B + k g •P(R=0)•E[Y | R=0], with b = (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 the pooled slope and k + B = E[Y²] = 1 within each group, regardless of that group's selection.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 4 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.
Some essential information could not be detected: statistical_test, sample_size, alpha_level, software

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(power_id = 1:2, power_type = c("unknown", "posthoc"
), statistical_test = c(NA, "other"), sample_size = c(NA, 320
), alpha_level = c(NA, 0.05), power = c(0.44, 0.482), effect_size = c(0.46, 
0.4), effect_size_metric = c("other", "other"), software = c(NA, 
"other")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", 
"data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE)
```

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "The search ran in three rounds on open data and required a complete-data Fisher-z difference with p < .05, and a fourth round checked the pick."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: R) re-screened two challengers against this pair, the psych::bfi personality data and a laboratory data set, and kept the pair: the first has no spread difference in Y (ratio 0.99), and the second shows no complete-data difference (p = 0.42).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.42", Sentence = "R) re-screened two challengers against this pair, the psych::bfi personality data and a laboratory data set, and kept the pair: the first has no spread difference in Y (ratio 0.99), and the second shows no complete-data difference (p = 0.42)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

ownership.dep_title: Derived Estimands Under Naive Multiple Imputation: Code, Data and Derivations for Three Papers
ownership.dep_description: A reproducible Monte Carlo study of how the choice of missing-data method affects inference about a continuous × continuous interaction (moderation) effect when one predictor is incomplete. Across small-to-moderate samples (N = 20–160), two missingness rates, and both MAR and MCAR mechanisms, we compare six methods — listwise deletion, mean imputation, regression imputation, and three multiple-imputation variants (naive, JAV, and substantive-model-compatible). The central finding is that "multiple imputation" names a family of procedures: naive imputation that omits the interaction attenuates the effect by roughly the fraction of data missing and its confidence-interval coverage worsens as the sample grows, while congenial (substantive-model-compatible) imputation recovers the interaction. This repository contains the base-R simulation code, figures, analytic derivations (verified), and the manuscript.
ownership.context: All simulation code, aggregated outputs, and the verification scripts named for each analytic result are openly available at https://osf.io/us4mb/. || The code behind the reported results is deposited at https://osf.io/us4mb/.

ownership.dep_title: The Cost of Naive Imputation to a Derived Estimand: An Exact Law, with the Square as Lead Case
ownership.dep_description: Multiple imputation is validated for variables; applied researchers report functions of them: a product, a square, a difference of correlations. An imputation model fitted to the columns cannot carry a relationship it does not contain, so the filled-in rows arrive stripped of it. The direction of the resulting bias is established. For the nonlinear terms studied here we are not aware of a published expression for its size as a function of the missing rate, and the literature we searched reaches that size by simulation, one design at a time. We derive it, as one law: under missingness completely at random the bias is the filled-in rows' failure to satisfy the analysis's own normal equations, converted into a coefficient error by the moments the analysis sees. The law reaches any derived term entering those equations, and not a ratio-and-transform estimand such as a difference of correlations. ownership.dep_description: Interaction hypotheses are central to psychology, and predictors are often incomplete. Standard guidance recommends multiple imputation (MI), yet "MI" denotes different procedures once the model contains a product term. We quantify how the imputation model governs recovery of a continuous × continuous interaction when one predictor is missing. The simulation spans N = 20–160, 20% and 40% missingness, and both missing-at-random (MAR) and missing-completely-at-random (MCAR), with 1000 replications per cell and Monte Carlo standard errors. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1528 columns across 142 data files.
#### Issues Identified
4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("p36imp_osf_bundle_20261007_v5.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MAR.csv", "p36imp_osf_bundle_20261007_v5.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MCAR.csv", "p36imp_osf_bundle_paper1_2026-10-27_2044_56f9ba37.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MAR.csv", "p36imp_osf_bundle_paper1_2026-10-27_2044_56f9ba37.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MCAR.csv" ), Column = c("rel_bias", "rel_bias", "rel_bias", "rel_bias"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 142 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

> source("R/simulation_functions.R")
> set.seed(20260801L)
> N <- 5e5
> REPS <- 6L
> M <- 5L
> PI <- 0.40
> lambda_of <- function(b1, b2, sig) b1^2 / (b1^2 + 2 * b2^2 + sig^2)
> kappa_at <- function(b1, b2, sig, reps = REPS) {
>   k <- numeric(reps)
>   for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
>     X <- rnorm(N)
>     Y <- b1 * X + b2 * X^2 + rnorm(N, sd = sig)
>     d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y)
>     d$X[runif(N) < PI] <- NA
>     P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d)
>     est <- numeric(M)
>     for (j in seq_len(M)) {
>       dd <- d; dd$X[is.na(d$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$X, P)
>       est[j] <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq,
>                                data = transform(dd, Xsq = X^2)))["Xsq"])
>     }
>     k[r] <- 1 - mean(est) / b2
>   }
>   c(kappa = mean(k), mcse = sd(k) / sqrt(reps))
> }

**`os.chdir()` in the code**
**1 script calls `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

Missing data are ordinary, and the standard advice for handling them is to use multiple imputation.
That advice is sound and it is also underspecified: "multiple imputation" names a family of procedures, and which member you get depends on choices that software makes for you.
This paper is about one such choice, in a setting where it decides the answer.
The setting is moderation by group.

A researcher asks whether two variables are more strongly related in one group than another -whether rumination tracks depressive symptoms more closely in a clinical sample than in controls, whether the link between sleep and mood is tighter in adolescents than in adults.
The estimand is a difference of correlations, which we take on the Fisher-z scale, ζ = z(ρ₁) -z(ρ₂), z(r) = artanh(r).
One of the two variables is incomplete.
The analyst imputes it and proceeds.
A plain correlation in a single bivariate-normal population cannot exhibit the failure we study, and that fact determines the design.
If (X, Y) is bivariate normal and X is missing-at-random (MAR) on Y, then imputing X from Y by linear regression is the correct conditional distribution.
The naive and the principled imputation model coincide, so there is no uncongeniality (no mismatch between the imputation model and the analysis) to find.
A partial correlation in a jointly normal world is safe for the same reason, provided the imputation model conditions on every variable the partial correlation adjusts for.
A reader who has met the congeniality literature (Meng, 1994) and expects trouble from any correlation estimand will not find it in this one.
text.formatted: A reader who has met the congeniality literature <ref type="bibr">(Meng, 1994)</ref> and expects trouble from any correlation estimand will not find it in this one.

text.text: The trouble appears when the analysis is group-heterogeneous while the imputation pools.
The analyst's model grants each group its own association.
The default imputation model grants each group its own mean and forces a common slope.
That omitted group × Y interaction is the precise analogue of the omitted product term that damages interaction estimates, and it is the object of this paper.
That default is not a hypothetical workflow.

Three widely used programs impute with main effects only unless told otherwise: SPSS imputes with INTERACTIONS=NONE, mice adds no interaction terms unless the user constructs them, and Stata requires an explicit include() or by().

Defaults vary by program, procedure, variable type and the formulas a user supplies, so we describe this as a common main-effects-only default workflow rather than as the behaviour of imputation software in general.
An analyst who accepts these defaults, having done nothing wrong by the letter of the standard advice, is running the pooled-slope model we show fails.
We simulate that model with Bayesian normal-regression draws (mice's norm).
The default draw mice uses for a numeric variable, predictive mean matching, keeps the same pooled slope, and we check it on one example only ( §Method).
The difference is attenuated by a factor we can write down.
The completed within-group covariance is a blend: the observed cases carry the group's own association, the imputed cases carry the pooled slope.

The pooled slope is common to both groups, so it cancels in the difference, and what survives is shrunk to the observed cases' share of the variance of Y. In the standardised design, the result is ζ → (1κ)•ζ, with κ = κ(π, ρ₁, ρ₂) depending mainly on the missing fraction π but also on the two correlations ( §Results 3a). κ is derived exactly, as a function of one-dimensional normal integrals (the selection moments of Y), verified step by step against simulation, and evaluated by quadrature for any missingness rate.
Below we call this expression the closed form: it is exact, but it is not elementary, because its integrals are evaluated numerically.
completely at random, necessary in the rate; and a manufactured difference from a true null when the groups differ in the spread of the complete variable.
The boundary converts the finding into an asymmetric reading rule rather than a general warning.

The premise is not ours. Graham (2009, p. 562) states that a correlation differing by group is an interaction, that the typical imputation model assumes the correlations are the same in both groups, and that imputing each group separately is a good way to allow for the difference.
text.formatted: The premise is not ours. <ref type="bibr">Graham (2009, p. 562)</ref> states that a correlation differing by group is an interaction, that the typical imputation model assumes the correlations are the same in both groups, and that imputing each group separately is a good way to allow for the difference.

text.text: Enders (2022, §10.2) states the premise in the same form and makes the same recommendation.
Neither gives the size of the cost of ignoring it.

We are not aware of a prior small-sample study comparing pooled against group-wise imputation for a between-group correlation difference, or of an analytic bias expression for this estimand -a statement about our searches, which we describe, not a claim that none exists.

The closest neighbour is Tilling et al. (2016): their stratified imputation is our group-wise arm under another name, and they report the same ultra-conservatism under a true null that we find one estimand over.
text.formatted: The closest neighbour is <ref type="bibr">Tilling et al. (2016)</ref>: their stratified imputation is our group-wise arm under another name, and they report the same ultra-conservatism under a true null that we find one estimand over.

text.text: We arrived at it independently.
We did not arrive at it first, and we say so.
§Related work gives the comparison in full, including what their design does not contain.
The mechanism, and where it has been studied

An analysis procedure is congenial to an imputation model when some single Bayesian model f can do both jobs at once: reproduce what the analyst reports, from the incomplete data and from the complete data alike, and carry a posterior predictive density for the missing values that is the imputer's density (Meng, 1994, p. 543, Definition 2).
text.formatted: An analysis procedure is congenial to an imputation model when some single Bayesian model f can do both jobs at once: reproduce what the analyst reports, from the incomplete data and from the complete data alike, and carry a posterior predictive density for the missing values that is the imputer's density <ref type="bibr">(Meng, 1994, p. 543, Definition 2)</ref>.

text.text: Two things follow that a shorter gloss loses.

Congeniality is a relation between an analysis and an imputation, not a property of the imputation by itself -the same filled-in data can be congenial to one analysis and uncongenial to another, as Meng remarks on that page.
And it asks the imputer and the analyst to agree with each other, not with the population: both can be wrong about the truth and congenial all the same.
Definition 2 defines the term and asserts nothing about validity.
Validity is a separate result, in Meng's §3, and the table below quotes the two statements of it that bear on this paper.

An analysis that lets two groups differ in association, filled from an imputation model that grants each group its own mean but a common slope, is uncongenial to it in a specific and diagnosable way, because the omitted term is the group × Y interaction.
The attenuation results below are variations on that mechanism, differing only in which estimand carries it.
Meng (1994) any Congeniality.
When imputer and analyst assume different models, multiple-imputation inference is not automatically valid.
In his §3.1 the imputer assumes more -this paper's case, a pooled model forcing one slope.
Meng attaches a condition.
"If the imputer's assessment is correct" (p. 546), the interval "has at least 1α coverage" (p. 546): too wide, not too narrow.
If it is incorrect, the estimator "is not consistent" (p. 545).
Here the assessment is that the groups share a slope and a residual variance.
If they do, the pooled arm is conservative ( §Results 4).
If they do not, it is in general inconsistent (the zero-slope case aside, and isolated rates can cancel), whether the correlations differ ( §Results 1-2) or are equal ( §Results 4b).

In §3.2, where the imputer assumes less, the inference is "valid and asymptotically efficient" (p. 547) theory von Hippel (2009) transformed variables Imputing a variable and then forming a transform of it attenuates the transform's coefficient.

text.text: Three of their findings touch this paper directly, and on two of them they have priority.
The first is that their stratified imputation is our group-wise arm.
They split the data by a fully observed, categorical variable in the interaction and impute within strata, which makes the omitted interaction unnecessary.
That is exactly the remedy we recommend, arrived at independently and credited here.

They also identify its boundary: stratification fails when the stratifying variable is continuous and split at its mean, because "within each half of the data set, there is still an association between Y and the interaction term XZ which is not being taken account of."
Our grouping variable is categorical, so our arm is not exposed to that failure -but the boundary is theirs.
The second is that they report overcoverage under a true null, which we did not know when we derived it.

Their summary of what is new includes the result, the last of its four bullets: when the interaction is truly zero and the imputation model omits it, confidence intervals overcover, reaching roughly 99% against a nominal 95% and rising at larger samples.
Their explanation is the one we give, that "the analyst is 'assuming' less than the imputer," which they attribute to Meng (1994) in their Discussion.
text.formatted: Their explanation is the one we give, that "the analyst is 'assuming' less than the imputer," which they attribute to <ref type="bibr">Meng (1994)</ref> in their Discussion.

text.text: Their overcoverage is the ultra-conservatism we report under the null in §Results 4, one estimand over.
We found it independently, but we did not find it first.
The third is that they report coverage worsening with sample size, in passing.
Comparing n = 2,000 with n = 20,000, they note that "coverage of the MI without interactions is lower" at the larger sample.
That observation occupies a single clause, its numbers sit in supplementary tables, and their own summary box does not mention it.
The observation is nonetheless reported, so any claim that the direction is undocumented would be false.
Seaman et al. (2012, p. 8) report the same direction for a squared term between N = 200 and 5,000, and Lüdtke et al.
(2020, Table 1) for a first-order coefficient of an interaction model between N = 100 and 1,000.
text.formatted: (2020, Table <ref type="table">1</ref>) for a first-order coefficient of an interaction model between N = 100 and 1,000.

text.text: Paper 1 of this series, More Data, Worse Inference (Shavit, 2026b; its second version is titled Missing-Data Imputation Can Miss an Interaction Effect or Raise a False Alarm), treats the same mechanism for a continuous × continuous interaction coefficient: there the imputation model omits the product term rather than the group × Y term, and the attenuation follows a factor of the same form.
We refer to it below where the two results differ.
Against that table, four things are not in it.
The first is a magnitude, in closed form.

Every study above establishes that an omitted interaction biases the corresponding estimate, and the simulation studies report its size at the settings they ran. von Hippel (2009) computes the size analytically for a square (Table 1, p. 275) and a product (Figure 1, p. 284), but reports example values, because the expressions "are too complicated to display" (p. 273).
text.formatted: Every study above establishes that an omitted interaction biases the corresponding estimate, and the simulation studies report its size at the settings they ran. von Hippel (2009) computes the size analytically for a square (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, p. 275) and a product (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, p. 284), but reports example values, because the expressions "are too complicated to display" (p. 273).

text.text: None gives the size in closed form for a correlation difference.
We give ζ → (1κ(π, ρ₁, ρ₂))•ζ with κ evaluable by quadrature for any missingness rate, and a general form covering unequal group sizes, means, variances and selection rates.
The second is the correlation-difference estimand itself, and the two-condition boundary it implies.
The literature above concerns regression coefficients and product terms, whereas a difference of correlations is a difference of separately rescaled slopes.
That rescaling makes the failure two-directional: the completed covariance and the completed variance are damaged through different channels, so the boundary requires two conditions rather than one.
The third is the direction in N, given as a curve.

Tilling et al. have the observation at two very large sample sizes for binary covariates, whereas we trace it across N = 40-320 with Monte Carlo standard errors, for continuous variables, together with the bias and standard-error decomposition that explains the direction rather than merely exhibiting it.
The fourth is the manufactured difference, and here prior work narrows what we may claim.

Yamaguchi, Ueno, Maruo and Gosho (2020) report that when treatment groups in a longitudinal trial are heteroscedastic, imputing them from a single pooled model biases the treatment-effect estimate and degrades coverage, and that imputing separately by group repairs it.
That is our mechanism, in which unequal group scale breaks a pooled imputation model, applied to a difference in means rather than in correlations.
We did not find it before deriving the correlation case, and it constrains what we may claim.
Our remaining claim is narrower and, we think, still worth reporting.
Theirs is bias in a non-null effect, whereas ours is a false positive from a true null, in which ρ₁ = ρ₂ exactly and the procedure invents a difference.

Theirs is simulation across variance structures, whereas ours is a closed form that predicts the size of the spurious effect and states a condition under which it vanishes, namely that the groups share a slope and, unless that shared slope is zero, a residual variance; the condition is sufficient, and necessary if the null must hold at every missing rate under missingness completely at random.
We also report the Type I error rising with sample size, from 0.03 at N = 80 to 0.31 at N = 640, which is the operational consequence and which we did not find reported anywhere.

Tilling et al.'s null-case result runs the other way, theirs being overcoverage where ours is a false positive, because binary covariates entering a common model do not carry separate scales and their design therefore cannot violate the condition that ours violates.
We should be plain about what "closed form" does and does not distinguish us.

Analytic bias expressions for multiple imputation are an established genre: Curnow et al. (2023) derive a maximum-bias expression for a regression coefficient when a collider is admitted to the imputation model as an auxiliary variable, and use it on real cohort data to bound the damage.
text.formatted: Analytic bias expressions for multiple imputation are an established genre: <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Curnow et al. (2023)</ref> derive a maximum-bias expression for a regression coefficient when a collider is admitted to the imputation model as an auxiliary variable, and use it on real cohort data to bound the damage.

text.text: The new element is the estimand, not the expression: a difference of correlations rather than a single coefficient, and a wholly manufactured effect from a true null rather than distortion of a real one.
Curnow et al. note in their Discussion that an exposure-confounder interaction would make their expression more complicated, and do not derive it.
Our group-wise arm is not new.
Saying precisely what is old delimits what we add.

Enders and Gottschall (2011) call it separate group imputation -it "imputes the data separately for each of the G subgroups," crediting von Hippel (2009) for stratify, then impute -and find it beats product term imputation, which admits group through code and product variables.
Their diagnosis is the one we formalise: product term imputation "implicitly uses a homoscedastic model," and fails when group variances differ.
Their pooled comparator is better specified than ours, which enters group as a main effect only.
A model with the product terms still fails, and that failure is stronger evidence for the mechanism than our own comparison provides.

Their bias, though, attenuates group differences toward the mean, raising Type II error, where our second result is a false positive from a true null -so they credit our attenuation and leave the manufactured difference untouched, as Tilling et al.'s null-case overcoverage does.
They also answer, in advance, the objection this design invites.

Enders and Gottschall note that their simulations were in one sense "rigged" against product term imputation, because the models always implied group differences in the population variances, and then report how large those differences were: F-max values, the ratio of the largest group variance to the smallest, spanning 1.10 to 2.00 across their three simulation models -differences "many researchers would consider … to be relatively small and well within the range of differences that would routinely appear in applied research."
Failing to preserve differences that small, they find, "can lead to substantial bias."
Our design is more austere than theirs.
Both variables are standard normal in both groups, so the F-max on either manifest variable is exactly 1, and an analyst who compared group variances would see nothing at all.

The heteroscedasticity is confined to the imputation residual, Var(X | Y) = 1 -ρ² g , which is 0.64 in the first group against 0.96 in the second: a ratio of 1.5, sitting inside the range they call routine.
The pooled model does not need visible heteroscedasticity to fail.
It needs only the kind that a table of group variances cannot show.
Group-wise imputation has been textbook advice since Graham (2009, p. 562) and Enders (2010, p. 267).
text.formatted: Group-wise imputation has been textbook advice since <ref type="bibr">Graham (2009, p. 562)</ref> and Enders (2010, p. 267).

text.text: Enders (2022, §10.2) recommends group-wise imputation for our exact situation -correlations by gender -on our exact premise: "a correlation that differs by gender implies a two-way interaction."
We are therefore not proposing the remedy; we are pricing the failure.
He compares group-wise against model-based imputation, both congenial, and reports similar, though not identical, estimates (p. 407).
The pooled, main-effects-only model that software gives by default is not among the arms he compares there, so that section reports no bias, coverage or rejection rate for it.
Ours remains the closed form, the estimand, the behaviour in N, and the boundary.

We ask how the choice of imputation model governs recovery of a between-group difference in correlation when one of the two correlated variables is incomplete, and we characterise the resulting bias analytically rather than only empirically.
Two questions organise the study: 1.

If the imputation model pools an association across groups -a common main-effects-only default, which enters group as a main effect -by how much is the between-group difference attenuated, and does that attenuation follow a law?
As the sample grows, what happens to confidence-interval coverage?
The study follows ADEMP (Morris, White & Crowther, 2019).
text.formatted: The study follows ADEMP <ref type="bibr">(Morris, White & Crowther, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Bias, coverage and the attenuation estimate κ in the simulation-grid tables carry Monte Carlo standard errors in parentheses.
Every rejection or detection rate comes from a stated number of replications R, so its Monte Carlo standard error is √(p(1 -p)/R).
Some values quoted in the prose, empirical standard errors, and the applied illustrations' estimates, κ and coverage are printed without one.
The estimand has to be a group difference A plain correlation in one bivariate-normal population cannot exhibit the failure we study, and saying why fixes the design.

§Introduction gives the reason: when (X, Y) is bivariate normal, regressing X on Y is the correct conditional distribution, so the naive and the congenial imputation models coincide and no uncongeniality can arise -for a plain correlation, and for a partial correlation when the imputation model conditions on every variable it adjusts for.
The split becomes real as soon as the analysis is group-heterogeneous while the imputation pools.
The analyst's model allows each group its own association.
The imputation model allows each group its own mean but forces a common X | Y slope.
The omitted group × Y interaction in the imputation model is the exact analogue of the omitted product term in the companion paper, and it makes the imputation uncongenial to the analysis.
Two equal-sized groups, g ∈ {1, 2}, with N/2 observations each.
Within group g, (X, Y) ~BVN(0, 0, 1, 1, ρ g ), so both variables are marginally standard normal in both groups and the groups differ only in the strength of association.
The estimand is the difference on the Fisher-z scale, ζ = z(ρ₁) -z(ρ₂), z(r) = artanh(r).
Designs (results/sequel_grid.csv): design ρ₁ ρ₂ ζ main 0.6 0.2 0.4904 robustness 0.7 0.3 0.5578

The null design ρ₁ = ρ₂ is treated analytically rather than by simulation; §Results explains why the closed form settles it exactly, and a 300-replication spot-check confirms it (results/sequel_spurious_twin.csv).

X is missing at random, with missingness depending on the fully observed Y: logit P(X missing | Y) = γ₀ + 0.7•Y, with γ₀ calibrated by root-finding so that the marginal missing fraction equals π ∈ {0.20, 0.40}.
Because Y is standard normal in both groups, the two groups lose the same expected fraction -a deliberate simplification.
The UCI example loses almost the same fraction from each group too (40.1% and 39.6% at π = 0.40, §5a).
The secondary iris report loses 27% and 53%, and §5d finds that this asymmetry adds almost none of the excess attenuation on its own.
Selection on Y alone is not an incidental choice.

It preserves E[X | Y, observed] = ρ g •Y, so the observed cases still carry each group's own association and the entire distortion is attributable to the imputation model rather than to selection on X.
N ∈ {40, 80, 160, 320}, R = 1000 replications per cell.
The range is chosen to span small to moderate two-group studies, and to make the behaviour in N visible rather than reporting a single N.
All four arms analyse the data the same way and differ only in what fills the missing values.

Full data the reference: analyse before missingness is imposed Listwise drop incomplete rows MI-pooled m = 20 proper draws from X | Y + group, group as a main effect only -a single pooled slope MI-group-wise m = 20 proper draws from X | Y fitted within each group MI-pooled is the arm under study.

It is not a straw man: main-effects-only imputation is a genuine default in three programs applied researchers use -SPSS imputes with INTERACTIONS=NONE, mice adds no interaction terms unless the user builds them, and Stata requires an explicit include() or by() to do otherwise.
Defaults differ across programs, procedures and variable types, so the claim is about this common workflow rather than about imputation software as a class.
An analyst who accepts these defaults gets a pooled slope, which is what defines the MI-pooled arm, and we call that arm the default below.
We draw from it by Bayesian normal regression (mice's norm). mice's own default draw for a numeric variable is predictive mean matching (van Buuren, 2018, §3.4.5).

On our UCI example at 40% missing, predictive mean matching shrinks the difference at least as much as the normal draw but detects it more often: in about 15% of maskings, against under 10% for the normal draw (verify/p36_verify_p2_pmm_default_2026-10-15.
Imputations are proper: each draw takes (β, σ) from the posterior of the Bayesian normal linear regression and then draws imputed values with residual noise.

Those draws carry the uncertainty the imputation model implies, which is a weaker property than calibrated inference about the correlation contrast, and the two come apart when the imputation model and the analysis disagree.

§Results 4 measures the gap at the one design where pooling gets the point estimate exactly right: the pooled arm's estimates still carry roughly half the congenial arm's sampling variability, and the pooled arm rejects a true null in at most 1 of 300 replications (rate 0.003) at each sample size, against a nominal 5%, about 15 rejections.
So the point estimate is not the only thing this arm can get wrong.
Within each group, r g is the Pearson correlation of the completed data, and the estimate is ζ = z(r1) -z(r2) with the Fisher-z Wald standard error SE = √( 1/(n₁ -3) + 1/(n₂ -3) ).

Multiple-imputation estimates are combined by Rubin's rules (Rubin, 1987) on the Fisher-z scale, backtransforming only for reporting, with the small-sample degrees of freedom of Barnard and Rubin (1999).
Fisher-z pooling is the standard procedure rather than our construction.

Enders (2022, p. 406) states it in three steps -transform each of the m correlations, average, back-transform -because "the sampling distribution of r becomes increasingly skewed as the population correlation moves away from zero."

White, Royston and Wood (2011, Table VIII) list the correlation among the statistics needing a transformation before Rubin's rules apply, and van Buuren (2018, §5.2.2) gives the z-scale variance 1/(n -3).

text.text: One caveat we state rather than bury: Barnard-Rubin has not been specifically validated for this estimand.
We use it as the conservative choice.
It widens intervals, so it cannot manufacture the coverage collapse we report.
If anything, it understates it.
For each cell the results table records bias on the z scale, empirical SE, RMSE, empirical 95% coverage and rejection rate (power under the alternative designs, Type I error under the null).
Bias, coverage and rejection rate carry Monte Carlo standard errors; empirical SE and RMSE do not.
We also report the empirical attenuation the fraction of the true difference that the method removes, which is the quantity the closed form predicts.

The pooled arm's bias is flat in N. It is not a small-sample artefact that more data will cure: eight times the sample changes the bias at π = 0.40 from -0.242 to -0.228, a shift of 0.014 against a combined Monte Carlo standard error of 0.0085 -1.7 standard errors, consistent with no change.
Group-wise imputation is unbiased throughout.
Listwise deletion loses efficiency against complete data (empirical SE 0.142 against 0.109 at N = 320, π = 0.40) but not against group-wise imputation (0.146).
The pooled arm's smaller 0.083 comes from its shrinkage, not from any gain in precision.
Listwise deletion also carries a small bias of its own, which the Listwise column above shows.

Selection on Y shrinks the observed-case variance of Y from 1 to v o = 0.907 at 40% missing, so each group's complete-case correlation is range-restricted, by the classical formula for direct selection on Y, to ρ g √v o ⁄ √(ρ g ²•v o + 1ρ g ²): 0.581 and 0.191 against 0.6 and 0.2.
The gap that opens, z(r cc ) -z(ρ g ), runs from -0.010 at ρ = 0.2 to -0.029 at ρ = 0.6.
It falls strictly as where both groups face the same selection the two attenuations cancel in the difference if and only if the two correlations are equal.
That is the null case of §4, not this design.

The probability limit here is -0.0194 on the z scale at π = 0.40 and -0.0132 at π = 0.20, a κ listwise of 0.040 against the pooled arm's 0.457 -under a tenth of the damage, and 3.2 to 4.2 Monte Carlo standard errors from zero in three of the four Listwise cells at N ≥ 160 (verify/p36_h1_listwise_rangerestriction_2026-10-07.py).

In panel B a single pooled imputation model supplies every missing value from one common slope, so the stronger association is pulled down and the weaker one pulled up.

(The panels show one realisation, so the pooled value sits near rather than on the closed-form plim of 0.27 quoted beneath them.)
The identification b = (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 is exact under this design and not in general.

It holds because the groups are equal-sized, Y is standard normal in both, and the missingness rule is therefore symmetric across them, so the pooled fit weights the two groups equally: verified numerically at N = 4 × 10⁵, where the pooled slope is 0.4011 on complete data and 0.4032 on the MAR-observed cases against a nominal 0.400.

If selection is asymmetric -as in the secondary iris report, and whenever the groups differ in the mean of Y -the pooled slope is neither (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 nor equal to its complete-data value, and it must be computed rather than assumed. §5a and §5c handle that case by evaluating the procedure directly rather than by substituting into this expression.

Two qualifications, both established below.

The identity is design-specific in its value but not its structure: Under the null, pooled imputation is not anti-conservative but ultra-conservative -its estimates have roughly half the sampling variability of the congenial arm, because pulling both groups toward a common slope suppresses the very variability the test needs.

A test that rejects a true null in at most 1 of 300 replications (rate 0.003), against a nominal 5%, is not a well-behaved test; it is miscalibrated in the other direction, and the attenuated point estimate, the halved power of §2 and this near-zero Type I rate are three faces of one invalid procedure rather than three separate findings.
Nothing below should be read as reassurance about the procedure.
This negative is part of the contribution, within its condition.

text.text: Under groupasymmetric MNAR on X a difference appears where none exists (row 3).
Symmetric MNAR is harmless, because both groups distort identically and the difference cancels (row 2).
So the asymmetry in an X-dependent mechanism breaks the boundary, as the proof's structure predicts.
Result 2: row 4 is not an exception, and its limit is exactly zero.
Opposite-direction selection removes high-X cases from group 1 and low-X cases from group 2, which sounds like the asymmetry that breaks row 3.
It is the reverse.

The pair (X, Y) is symmetric under (X, Y) → (-X, -Y), and both groups are calibrated to the same rate, so group 2's observed cases lose exactly the association group 1's lose and the difference cancels in every arm.
Quadrature over the selection law returns plim ζ = 0 to 10⁻³⁰ for listwise deletion and for group-wise imputation.

The pooled arm inherits it because the two groups' observed-case fits are mirror images (verify/p36_verify_p2_mech4_plim_2026-10-08.py; the control sets group 2's slope to zero, which is mechanism 3, and recovers -0.0429 rather than zero).
The printed +0.0038, +0.0018 and +0.0039 are therefore single-draw noise around a true zero, as multiples of 2.1, 1.3 and 1.8 already suggest.
The boundary breaks on a group difference in the selection, not on selection on X as such.
Result 3: the imputation does not produce the distortion, and pooling displaces least.
Listwise deletion is the most displaced arm (-22.5 SE).
Selection on X restricts X's range in group 1 and attenuates that group's correlation, so the estimand is compromised before any imputation happens.
Group-wise imputation, fitted to those same selected cases, carries a displaced limit of its own (-16 SE), close to listwise's and not equal to it.
Quadrature over the selection law gives the two limits exactly, -0.0429 and -0.0369 (verify/p36_verify_p2_mnar_plims_2026-10-07.py), so neither arm reproduces one common compromised quantity.
That 0.0060 gap is exact rather than estimated.
The single realisations in the table, each within about one standard error of its own limit, could not have settled it.
Pooled imputation is the least displaced (-14.1 SE).
It shrinks the two groups toward each other as it always does, and here that shrinks a spurious difference toward zero.
Result 4: Type I error at N = 320 (R = 1000) inverts the usual ordering.
Under the worst mechanism the pooled arm rejects at 0.004, while group-wise imputation reaches 0.073, 2.8 MCSE above nominal.
The congenial arm is the anti-conservative one here because its own displaced limit (Result 3) is large against its intervals.
Pooled imputation remains ultra-conservative, because its displacement is small relative to its intervals.
The low rate is not an argument for pooling.
Under MNAR on X the damage is done before any imputation runs.
None of the three procedures tested here models X-dependent selection, so none of them could repair it.
A repair would need a selection model this design does not identify, and these four mechanisms neither supply one nor rule one out.
Scope.

Row 1 of the §4 table survives this stress test, stated precisely: where the groups share both a slope and a residual variance, pooled imputation did not inflate a group difference relative to a congenial analysis of the same data under any of the four mechanisms tested here.
Under MAR on Y that is a proved statement, since the closed form cannot move the null at all.
Under MNAR on X it is a numerical finding on four mechanisms, not a theorem.
The pooled estimate moves, but less than the alternatives do, and we have no derivation covering arbitrary selection functions.
Drop the shared-slope condition and the rule fails outright (row 3 of the reading-rule table).

With equal correlations and a two-fold difference in the spread of Y, the pooled plim is -0.1210 while the congenial arm sits at -1.1 × 10⁻¹⁶ (results/sequel_manufacture_scale.csv). §4b is that case. 4b.
Pooled imputation can manufacture a difference when the groups differ in scale Source: R/drv004_general.R, R/verify_drv004_general.R.
The general form ( §Theory, "The general form") shows the boundary needs the groups to share the slope β g = ρ g •σ Xg /σ Yg and the residual variance τ² g = σ² Xg (1 -ρ² g ) -not the correlation.
In the standardised design all three are the same condition, which is how we came to state it as a claim about correlations.
They are not the same in general.

Take ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40 exactly -no true difference -with σ X = 1 in both groups, MAR on Y at 40% calibrated within each group so the rates match, and let the groups differ only in the spread of Y. Matching the rates does not match the strength: the selection model acts on the raw outcome, so the group with the wider Y is selected at a higher effective standardised strength, and the contrast below carries that alongside the scale difference.
Varying σ X instead is much weaker and not even monotone in sign (+0.0021 at a two-fold ratio, -0.0387 at four-fold), because it moves β g and τ² g together and the two effects partly cancel.
Scale heterogeneity in the incomplete variable is therefore the mild case.
Heterogeneity in Y -the variable selection acts onmanufactures the difference.
No case above changes the residual variance with the slope held fixed, so none of them shows that the second condition does any work on its own.
Scaling σ X and σ Y by the same factor holds β g exactly fixed while τ² g = σ² Xg (1 -ρ² g ) grows with it.
The completed covariance then comes out exactly right -b equals each group's own slopeand the entire distortion arrives through Var g (X*): Simulation confirms it, across a full grid (Figure 6).

At N = 640 with 40% missing and a three-fold standard-deviation ratio -a nine-fold variance ratio -31% of analyses declare a correlation difference that does not exist, six times the nominal rate.
Smaller spread differences displace the estimate without inflating Type I error.
At a 1.5-fold ratio the plim is -0.074, but the pooled arm stays at or below nominal through N = 640 (0.033); the rate first exceeds nominal at a two-fold ratio and N = 640 (0.149).
For scale, the largest variance ratio Enders and Gottschall (2011, p. 51) describe as routine in applied research is 2.00, a 1.41-fold standard-deviation ratio.

(One of the eighteen sample-size steps in those six configurations is non-monotone -ratio 2, π = .20, between N = 160 and N = 320 -a drop of 0.008 against a combined MCSE of 0.007, i.e.
Monte Carlo noise, reported rather than smoothed.
Over the full grid of eight configurations, the two controls included, four of twenty-four steps fall: three inside the controls, where no rise is expected, and that one.)
The manufactured difference is the coverage collapse again, pointing the other way
The mechanism is the one from §2 and the arithmetic is identical.
The manufactured ζ is fixed in N while its standard error falls like 1/√N, so the ratio of the two grows without bound and the true null is rejected more and more often.
Under the alternative that process destroys coverage; under the null it destroys Type I control.
Both are the same fixed-bias-with-shrinking-interval structure, and both get worse with exactly the thing researchers use to make results more trustworthy.
The practical consequence is sharper than the attenuation result.
A small study in these designs will usually not detect the artefact.
A large one will report it as a significant finding.

As N → ∞ the rejection rate goes to 1 whenever the pooled procedure's limiting contrast is a fixed nonzero number, because that defect stays put while the interval shrinks like 1/√N. The asymptotic claim therefore needs a nonzero limiting contrast, and unequal group variances are not sufficient for one.
Heterogeneity in Y, the variable selection acts on, produces it here: a two-fold ratio in σ Y manufactures -0.1210 against the +0.0021 a two-fold ratio in σ X manufactures ( §4b above).
And two groups with no association at all keep the contrast at exactly zero, at every rate and at any spread ratio, because both then share the slope zero ( §Appendix).
The limit of 1 is an asymptotic statement about the rejection probability, not a guarantee about any one finite sample.

Applied illustration: a group difference in psychological data, mostly lost after default imputation Sources: results/sequel_applied_uci.csv (R = 2000), results/sequel_applied_plim_exact.csv, results/sequel_applied_plim.csv; figure results/sequel_applied.png.
Secondary report ( §5c-5d): results/sequel_applied_iris.csv, results/sequel_applied_plim_exact_iris.csv.
The UCI Drug Consumption (Quantified) data (Fehrman et al., 2015) record NEO-FFI-R personality scores, sensation seeking (ImpSS) and education for 1,885 adults.

Openness to experience and sensation seeking are positively associated in each education group, and the strength differs: r = 0.243 among respondents with a master's degree (n = 283) and 0.457 among respondents who left school at 18 (n = 100).

The complete-data Fisher-z contrast is ζ full = z(0.243) -z(0.457) = -0.2465, SE 0.1178, z = -2.09, p = 0.036significant at the uncorrected 0.05 level, so an analyst with complete data reports the difference.
As §Method says, the pair came out of a screen and a multiplicity-corrected test would not reach significance.
We use it to illustrate any moderation-by-group question with one incomplete measure, and make no claim about education.
Neither end of the scales nor a few respondents drive the contrast.
At most 1% of either group scores at the floor or ceiling of openness.
The spread difference holds on a robust scale (median absolute deviation, MAD, ratio 1.70, against 1.45 for the standard deviation).
Spearman correlations agree (0.236 and 0.428), and removing any one respondent moves ζ by at most 19%.
A single deletion does lift p above .05 in 6 of the 383 cases, the largest to .070, as a result at p = .036 would lead one to expect (R/p36_paper2_uci_robustness.R).
We treat the complete-data value as the benchmark, impose MAR missingness on sensation seeking (logit P = a + 0.7•z(openness)) 2000 times, and re-estimate.

At 20% missing it detects the difference in 18%, against 41% and 46%.
The default model does not erase the estimate here.
It shrinks it toward zero, and that is enough to lose four in five of the detections group-wise imputation keeps.

The share of intervals containing ζ full stays at or near 1 for every arm, because the benchmark is the sample's own value and every interval is built for sampling variability the benchmark does not have.
That share is not confidence-interval coverage of a population value and is not compared with 0.95.
On these data the damage shows in detection, not in that share.

The subsections take the result apart in two steps. §5a sets these masking results beside the limits in a normal population fitted to the data. §5b splits the pooled arm's displacement into §3's shrinkage and §4b's manufactured part (rows 2, 3 and 5 of the §4 table). §5c and §5d repeat both steps on iris.
The population the quadrature evaluates is a bivariate normal fitted to the two groups' means, spreads, correlations and sizes.
The UCI scores are the dataset authors' quantified values and are discrete (sensation seeking takes 11 values), so every "exact" figure below is exact in that fitted population and not in the sample.
Group-wise imputation is again exactly unbiased in the fitted population.
Pooled imputation removes about a quarter of the difference at 40% missing, half of what a balanced design with the same two correlations loses ( §5b).

Selection is nearly symmetric here: the two groups have almost the same mean openness, so the rule removes 40.1% and 39.6% of their values, and the pooled slope the imputation model targets is 0.306 at both rates against 0.307 on complete data.
A simulated plim (R/verify_applied_plim.R, N = 2 × 10⁶) gives 0.126 and 0.227, inside its own Monte Carlo noise of about 0.007 in κ.
(i) A finite-sample offset that is not an imputation effect.
The finite-sample estimates differ from their plims, in the opposite direction from iris.

Listwise and group-wise κ are negative at π = .40 (-0.092 and -0.102), against simulated plims (R/verify_applied_plim.R, N = 2 × 10⁶) of +0.083 and -0.005, the second of them zero in the exact evaluation above: in the actual sample, deleting sensation-seeking values according to openness moves the estimated difference away from zero.

An MCAR control, deleting at the same per-group rates completely at random, returns κ of -0.004 and -0.000 for listwise deletion against -0.036 and -0.095 under the MAR rule in the control's own paired draws (the table's -0.033 and -0.092 come from separate draws), so the offset is MAR range restriction acting on the real scores, not a deletion artefact and not an imputation effect.
(ii) The increment pooling adds, against the closed form.

The incremental attenuation that pooling adds on top of group-wise imputation is the quantity the closed form predicts: π plim (pooled -group-wise), exact observed at N = 383 difference 0.20 0.1323 0.1390 +0.0068 0.40 0.2343 0.2840 +0.0497
At 20% missing the quadrature predicts the increment to within 0.007, as it does for iris.
At 40% it under-predicts by 0.050, five times the iris discrepancy.
We report the larger gap rather than average it away.
The fitted normal population approximates these discrete scores less well than it approximates sepal measurements, which is consistent with the gap but does not establish its source.
We have not isolated it.

On these data the two mechanisms pull against each other §3 proves that pooled imputation shrinks a real difference, and §4b proves that it manufactures one when the groups differ in the spread of Y. Here they differ 1.45-fold: within-group standard deviations of openness are 0.883 and 1.277 in the shared standardised units, and the ratio of median absolute deviations, 1.70, says the gap is not driven by a few extreme scores.

Both conditions hold, so we run the three-design decomposition that §5d sets out in full for iris, with a script written for these data (verify/p36_verify_p2_uci_decomposition_2026-10-13.py, N = 2 × 10⁶ per replication, 36 replications, the dataset's own group sizes, no code shared with R/applied_plim_exact.R).
Design A is the UCI fit, B the balanced design with the same two correlations, C the UCI fit with both correlations set to their mean, so its true contrast is zero.
Displacement is signed: positive means the estimate is pulled toward zero.
The manufactured difference reproduces at a 1.45-fold spread ratio, with the opposite sign to iris.
In design C, with no true difference, pooled imputation still produces a contrast of 0.062 at 40% missing.

The group with the larger spread in openness, those who left school at 18, is also the group with the stronger correlation, and §4b's mechanism raises the completed correlation in the larger-spread group.
So the manufactured contrast points the same way as the real one and cancels about half the shrinkage: the real design's displacement of 0.058 is half the balanced design's 0.113.
The two mechanisms still add, to within 0.007, and the control fires: equalising the spreads as well as the correlations drops design C to 0.0000 and leaves B plus that design missing A by 0.056.
Design C's common correlation is again a free choice, and setting it to either group's own value moves the π = 0.40 residual to -0.012 and +0.026.
So the demonstration reproduces as a mechanism, not as an aggravation.
On these data the manufactured difference masks part of the attenuation.
On iris ( §5d), where the group with the weaker correlation has the larger spread, it stacks on top of it.
The spread of Y is fully observed, so an analyst can check which of the two directions applies before imputing, though not whether a study is cleared ( §Discussion).
Earlier versions of this paper used base-R iris, and we keep it as a second report because its groups differ in spread more than the UCI groups do, and in the other direction.

Sepal length and sepal width are positively associated within each species, and the strength differs: r = 0.743 in setosa and 0.457 in virginica (N = 100, 50 per species), so the complete-data Fisher-z contrast is ζ full = z(0.743) -z(0.457) = 0.4623, SE 0.2063, z = 2.24, p = 0.025almost exactly the simulated design value, and significant.
An analyst with complete data reports the species difference.

The pooled model does more than cost power.
It removes the effect.
The iris quadrature carries the same caveat as §5a.
Each dataset is one worked application, repeatedly masked -a transport check, not replication across datasets or data-generating processes.
The population the quadrature evaluates is a bivariate normal fitted to iris, so every "exact" figure below is exact in that fitted population and not in the finite, non-normal sample.
The applied κ of 0.850 at π = 0.40 is far above the balanced design's closed-form 0.4567, because iris carries both of this paper's mechanisms at once.
The two species differ in correlation, which §3 shows pooled imputation shrinks.

They also differ in the spread of sepal length -within-species standard deviations of 0.373 and 0.673 in the shared standardised units, a 1.80-fold ratio -which is §4b's condition for pooled imputation to manufacture a difference where none exists.
Both act in the same direction, and §5d below shows that on this dataset they add.
The selection is also asymmetric: virginica has longer sepals, so the same missingness rule strips 53% of its values against setosa's 27%.
That asymmetry is real, and on its own it accounts for almost none of the excess -the control in §5d holds it in full and removes it anyway.

R/applied_plim_exact.R evaluates the identical procedure by quadrature -generalising the closed form to unequal group means, SDs and missingness rates, which the symmetric version does not cover -giving the plim exactly: π plim κ, pooled plim κ, group-wise 0.20 0.3381 -4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ 0.40 0.7001 -1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ Two features of this table matter.
First, the group-wise plim is exactly zero to machine precision although selection is strongly asymmetric.
In the fitted normal population, group-wise imputation is not approximately unbiased for this estimand but exactly unbiased, which no simulation can establish.
That is a property of the model-based mechanism check, not of the iris sample itself: complication (i) below reports the offset the real, non-normal data carry on top of it.
Second, the pooled slope the imputation model targets is far from the symmetric-design value (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2 = 0.600.
It is 0.
Two effects separate them, and the larger one has nothing to do with missing data.

The pooled model X ~Y + species estimates a variance-weighted average of the two within-species slopes -1.81 and 0.52 in the shared standardised units -and that average already sits at 0.826 on the complete data.

Selection on Y then accounts for the rest: it strips more of virginica, whose sepals are the longer ones, so the species that keeps more rows weighs more heavily in the fit and the slope rises from 0.826 to 0.953.
At π = .40 the complete-data gap accounts for 64% of the distance from 0.600 and selection for 36%.
At π = .20 the split is 78% and 22% (verify/p36_n7_iris_pooled_slope_2026-10-07.py).

So §Theory's asymmetric-selection caveat applies on top of a comparator that was never right for this dataset: a slope stops matching a correlation as soon as the groups' spreads differ, and here they differ 1.80-fold.
A simulated plim (R/verify_applied_plim.R) agrees to 0.0017 and 0.0013, which is its proper role -a check on the exact computation, not the source of the number.
Listwise deletion, not covered by the quadrature module, has a simulated plim κ of -0.013/-0.013.
(i) A common finite-sample offset.
Every arm at N = 100 sits above its plim by a common amount (+0.08 at π = .20, +0.15 at π = .40) -including the two arms whose plim is ≈ 0, so it cannot be an imputation effect.

An MCAR control on the real sample, deleting at the same per-species rates but completely at random, returns κ = +0.003 and -0.011, against +0.065 and +0.133 for that same listwise arm under the mechanism -a twentieth and a twelfth of the size.
The offset is therefore MAR range restriction acting on the actual iris points.

The fitted normal population understates it, which is consistent with, but does not establish, a departure from bivariate normality: an exactly normal sample of this size and these moments produces a listwise offset this large in fewer than one sample in ten.
The offset is a property of the data and affects every method alike.
(ii) The increment pooling adds, against the closed form.

The closed form therefore describes the incremental attenuation that pooling adds on top of group-wise imputation, and that increment agrees with the plim almost exactly: π plim (pooled -group-wise), exact observed at N = 100 difference 0.20 0.3381 0.3442 +0.0061 0.40 0.7001 0.6902 -0.0099 Evaluated on a normal population matched to this dataset's unequal means, spreads and deletion fractions, the law derived in §Theory predicts the damage done on the real, not-quite-normal dataset to within 0.010.
A single exactly normal dataset of this size and these moments would vary by a standard deviation of about 0.06, so the agreement is closer than the data can certify.

It is worth having, but it cannot by itself identify which mechanism did the damage: both sides of it -the quadrature and the simulation -are computed on the same design, carrying the same unequal means, unequal spreads and unequal deletion rates, so a comparison between them cannot separate §3's shrinkage from §4b's manufactured difference.
The check that can separate them is in §5d.
Two datasets are still not empirical generality, and we do not claim it.

A plim estimated by simulation gives 0.0005 and 0.0059 here, which is too flattering: the simulated plim itself moves by 0.004 between N = 10⁶ and N = 2 × 10⁶, so its own Monte Carlo noise is the size of the agreement it is being used to demonstrate.
The quadrature values carry no such noise and the honest figure is 0.010.
The residual gap is smaller than the variation between exactly normal datasets of this size, so it cannot be attributed to the real data's departure from the fitted normal model.
On iris the two mechanisms add iris meets the conditions for both of the paper's failures, so §5c cannot say how much of the applied damage belongs to each.

Write displacement for how far the pooled estimate falls below the truthζ full minus the probability limit of ζ , so §5c's κ times 0.4623 -and compare three designs, each simulated from the procedure at N = 2 × 10⁶ per replication, 36 replications (verify/p36_verify_p2_applied_decomposition_2026-10-06.py, written from the method and sharing no code with R/applied_plim_exact.R): • A, the real design -the iris fit exactly as above.
• B, the balanced design -the same two correlations, both species standard normal with equal means.
This is the design §Theory derives its closed form for, so B is §3's mechanism acting alone.
• C, the null design -the iris fit with the two correlations set equal to their mean, so the true contrast is zero and any displacement that appears is manufactured.
This is §4b's mechanism acting alone.
Monte Carlo standard errors are at or below 0.0003 throughout, so the residuals are far larger than the noise and are being reported rather than smoothed.

The instrument reproduces §5c's quadrature where the two overlap: the same script returns plim κ of 0.3378 and 0.6999 against the quadrature's 0.3381 and 0.7001, and B's implied balanced κ of 0.4488 at π = 0.40 sits 0.0004 from the quadrature's balanced value.
Neither mechanism reproduces the applied result alone.
At π = 0.40, §3's balanced displacement falls 0.116 short of the real design and §4b's manufactured displacement falls 0.201 short.
At π = 0.20 they fall 0.044 and 0.099 short.
Added, they land within 0.007 and 0.013.

So the applied attenuation is roughly two parts shrinkage of a real difference to one part manufacture of a false one, and reporting only the first would understate how a reader's own data could go wrong: a dataset with the spread ratio and no true difference still gets a displacement of 0.12 at 40% missing.
The decomposition is a numerical finding on one dataset, not a theorem.
Nothing we derive says the two mechanisms superpose, and the comparison carries one free choice -design C's common correlation.
Setting it to setosa's 0.743 moves the π = 0.40 residual to -0.025 and to virginica's 0.457 moves it to +0.019, so the residual's size depends on that choice at the same order as the residual itself.

All three settings of design C's common correlation give the same conclusion, which no single-mechanism account can give: the sum stays within 0.025 of the real design, while either mechanism alone misses by 0.10 or more.
The control that makes the decomposition discriminating does fire.

Equalise the two species' sepal-length spreads as well as their correlations, keeping the unequal mean lengths and therefore the asymmetric deletion rates almost intact (0.267 / 0.532 at π = 0.40, against 0.266 / 0.534), and the manufactured displacement collapses from 0.1227 to 0.0001.
B plus that design misses the real one by 0.116 -the whole §4b contribution.
Two things follow.

The decomposition is not an identity that any pair of designs would satisfy, and the asymmetric deletion rates §5c once credited with the excess produce essentially none of it on their own: the 1.80-fold spread ratio produces the excess.

The observed cases contribute the group's own association ρ g , weighted by A. The imputed cases contribute the pooled slope b, weighted by B. And b is by construction common to both groups, so when we take the difference between groups it cancels:
The between-group difference in covariance is carried by the first term, shrunk to the observed-case share A, which is approximately 1π.
The offset term is small but not zero: at ρ = (.6, .2) and π = .40 it is -0.0153 against the first term's 0.2329, 6.6% of it.
"Shrunk to A" is therefore the leading behaviour of this standardised design and not an identity.

The Appendix gives the exact decomposition, which carries no separate offset and in which the weight is the observed-case variance component which is 0.2176 at π = .40: the first term plus the offset.

Everything the paper reports follows from that one line: the difference is carried only by the cases that were actually seen, and the cases that were imputed have been told, by the model, that the groups share one slope.

The rows that were seen contribute each group's own association ρ g with weight A, the rows that were filled in contribute the single pooled slope b with weight B, and A + B = E[Y²] = 1 at every rate -so the missing fraction decides nothing except how one unit of weight is split between the two.
Drawn, the blend is two curves falling onto one horizontal line, and differencing removes that line outright.

The figure carries the caveat with it: the exact difference and the (ρ₁ -ρ₂)•A reference are two separate curves, so the space between them -the offset term, 6.6% of the first term at π = .40 -is visible rather than asserted.
