The result is the plim itself, which Steps 1-5 compute from the completed moments and Step 7 evaluates. κ depends on π and on both correlations, and we write κ(π) only where the correlation pair is held fixed.
Verified: r₁ = 0.5126, r₂ = 0.2892 against theoretical 0.5120 and 0.2905; ζ = 0.2685 against 0.2664, i.e. κ = 0.4524 against the predicted 0.4567.

The moments above are one-dimensional integrals of a standard normal density against a logistic weight, so κ can be evaluated by quadrature to machine tolerance rather than by simulation (zeta_plim_exact() in R/drv004_closedform.R).
Quadrature matters here because the Monte Carlo alternative carries about ±0.01 of noise on κ, which is enough to hide κ's dependence on the correlation pair.
That dependence is real -see §Results 3a.
The self-check in R/drv004_closedform.R, run by R/sequel_kappa_curve.R and by the deposit's make verify, asserts both evaluators against the four verified designs.
§Results 2 reports that nominal 95% coverage of ζ falls from 0.992 at N = 40 to 0.703 at N = 320, and the Discussion explains it as a fixed bias divided by a shrinking interval.

That explanation is a theorem, stated with its hypotheses in the companion paper on the interaction (Paper 1, Appendix §G, Result G1): if the estimate converges in probability to a constant T*, the reported half-width converges in probability to a constant h*, and the asymptotic defect Δ = |T* -T| against the target T satisfies h* < Δ, then coverage tends to zero.
text.formatted: That explanation is a theorem, stated with its hypotheses in the companion paper on the interaction (Paper 1, Appendix §G, Result G1): if the estimate converges in probability to a constant T*, the reported half-width converges in probability to a constant h*, and the asymptotic defect Δ = |T* -T| against the target T satisfies h* < Δ, then coverage tends to zero.

text.text: The proof is three lines and turns on nothing more than the reverse triangle inequality and a union bound.
The theorem needs the strict inequality, and that is why we quote all three cases.

Result G1 is a trichotomy in the comparison between the settled half-width h* and the asymptotic defect Δ: (a) h* < Δ sends coverage to zero; (b) h* > Δ sends it to one; (c) h* = Δ determines nothing, and every value in [0, 1] is attainable as the limit.
text.formatted: Result G1 is a trichotomy in the comparison between the settled half-width h* and the asymptotic defect Δ: (a) h* < Δ sends coverage to zero; (b) h* > Δ sends it to one; (c) h* = Δ determines nothing, and every value in [0, 1] is attainable as the limit.

text.text: So a fixed, non-vanishing defect does not by itself destroy coverage.
Case (b) is the counterexample: hold Δ fixed, let the reported interval settle at a width above it, and coverage goes to one rather than to zero.

Case (a) therefore needs both halves -a defect that does not vanish and a width that settles strictly below it -and the word strictly carries weight, because at the boundary h* = Δ a half-width approaching Δ from below more slowly than the estimate's sampling error shrinks drives coverage to zero, one approaching from above as slowly drives it to one, one approaching at the sampling-error rate leaves it anywhere strictly between, and one approaching faster than that rate (or sitting at Δ) holds it at one half.
Quoting only case (a) would leave a reader with the much stronger and false reading that bias alone is enough.
Take T = ζ, the true Fisher-z contrast, and which at π = 0.40 and ρ = (.6, .2) is 0.4567 ×0.490 = 0.224 -a fixed number, not something that shrinks with the sample.

The reported interval is built by Rubin's rules on the Fisher-z scale, and its half-width goes to zero in probability because the m completed-data estimates share a probability limit, the within-imputation variance 1/(n₁ -3) + 1/(n₂ -3) vanishes deterministically, and the Barnard-Rubin multiplier is bounded in probability rather than convergent to a constant (Paper 1, §G, Result G2).

Boundedness is all Result G2 asks of it, and the multiplier stays random in the limit because the fraction of missing information does: with m fixed at 20, the multiplier's fifth to ninety-fifth percentiles hold at 1.965 to 1.982 from n = 160 to n = 20480 rather than narrowing (verify/p36_n1_p2_multiplier_2026-10-07.py).
So h* = 0 < Δ and coverage tends to zero.
text.formatted: So h* = 0 < Δ and coverage tends to zero.

text.text: ∎ Three qualifications matter for how §Results 2 should be read.

The defect must be written as a difference, not as a ratio, at the true null. κ(π) is defined as (ζ -plim ζ )/ζ and is undefined when ζ = 0, which is exactly the manufactured-contrast case of §Results 4b.
There Δ = |plim ζ -0| is a manufactured nonzero number and the corollary still applies, but only in the difference form.

The conclusion is a limit, not a direction at every N. Coverage tending to zero does not imply that it falls at every sample size, and the grid in §Results 2 should be described as showing when the collapse arrives rather than as evidence of monotone decay.
And κ(π) = 0 is not a safe harbour.
If the groups share slope and residual variance, the defect vanishes and this corollary says nothing -in either direction.
A separate argument, not this one, would have to establish that coverage is then correct.
Everything above assumes the design of the simulation: equal groups, Y standard normal in both, identical selection.
Real data satisfy none of that.

The Appendix drops all three and restates the boundary in the form the algebra actually supportsif the groups share both the slope β g and the residual variance τ² g , then a zero contrast stays zero, and so does any contrast, zero or not: plim ζ = ζ, for any selection on Y, provided X depends on Y linearly with a residual variance that does not change with Y in each group (the Appendix's model; normality itself is not needed).

Those two conditions are sufficient, and -for two groups under missingness completely at random, once the common rate varies -necessary: at a fraction common to both groups, the contrast survives at every rate only when the slope is shared and the residual variance is too, with the one trivial exception that neither group has any association at all.
That holds for any positive group shares and any positive outcome variances, equal or not.
The Appendix proves this converse by hand, in three short cases.

The Appendix also records the object underneath both statements: under missingness completely at random, and with an imputer whose limiting law does not change with the missing rate (as this paper's do), the pooled moments are straight lines in the missing rate, so the bias is the imputed rows' failure to satisfy the analysis's own normal equations.
That failure being zero is normal-equation compatibility, a condition on the imputed rows against the population.
Congeniality in Meng's (1994) sense asks only that imputer and analyst agree with each other, which can hold when their common model is wrong.
text.formatted: Congeniality in <ref type="bibr">Meng's (1994)</ref> sense asks only that imputer and analyst agree with each other, which can hold when their common model is wrong.

text.text: A correlation is a ratio of those moments rather than a coefficient in them, which is why this paper's estimand needs the further step the Appendix takes by hand.
That step runs one way only: correct completed moments are sufficient for a correct correlation contrast, not necessary.

In the trivial exception above, with no association in either group and unequal residual variances, the completed variances are wrong (7/4 and 13/4 against true values of 1 and 4 in one exact case at half the data missing), yet both completed correlations equal the true value of zero.
The special case makes the two conditions look like one, which is how we came to state the boundary as a claim about equal correlations.
§Results 4b reports what happens when they come apart.

Where it is used What happens without it Missingness depends on Y only Step 1 E[X|Y,R=1] ≠ ρ g •Y, so the observed part no longer carries ρ g cleanly and the complete-case slope becomes biased as well.

Selection on Y already biases the complete-case correlation: it shrinks Var(Y | R=1) to 0.907 at 40% missing and range-restricts each group's correlation with it, which displaces the contrast by -0.019 ( §Results 1) Within-group bivariate normality Steps 1, 5 the conditional mean may be non-linear; the pooled-slope mechanism survives, the closed form does not.

Normality is not required for the common-rate MCAR boundary theorem, which needs only finite positive-definite within-group covariances, group-specific intercepts in the fitted imputer, and the population projection slope and residual variance.

Interval calibration is not covered Assumed Where it is used What happens without it Equal groups, common Y distribution, symmetric selection Steps 3-6 of the special case only superseded by §"The general form", which drops all of it: b becomes a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes and the identity becomes 𝒜 g + ℬ g = σ² Yg Var(Y) = 1 Step 6 rescaling only; correlations are scale-invariant Nothing in the mechanism requires the missingness rate to be equal across groups, and nothing requires the two correlations to have the same sign -the (0.5, -0.1) design is verified at step level too.

If the analysis lets groups differ, the imputation model must let them differ in the same way, unless the groups share the conditional slope and residual variance ( §Results 4), which no published table can show.
For a between-group difference in association, this means imputing within group -or using an imputation model that gives each group its own conditional slope and its own residual variance.
Adding group as a main effect is not a partial fix but no fix at all, because it leaves the entire attenuation in place: what is pooled is the slope, not the means.

Adding the group × predictor interaction to one homoscedastic regression is a partial fix and not an equivalent one, which is worth saying because it is the easier thing to do in standard software: it frees the slopes and still pools the residual variance, so the completed variance stays wrong whenever the groups' residual variances differ, and that is one of the two mechanisms this paper reports.

At β = (0.8, 1.3), τ² = (0.5, 1.4) and variances of Y of 1 and 4, the interaction-only model misses a group's correlation by up to 0.111, while the same model with equal residual variances is exact (verify/p36_verify_p2_exact_recovery_2026-10-02.
The cost of doing so is small.
Over the ten cells of the κ-curve anchor run, group-wise imputation held bias within [-0.009, +0.017] and coverage within [0.942, 0.968].
The main grid adds two cells outside that bias range: +0.024 (Monte Carlo SE 0.013) at π = 0.20 and N = 40, and -0.011 (0.007) at π = 0.40 and N = 160.

At N = 320 and π = 0.40 it costs variance against the pooled arm (empirical SE 0.146 against 0.083) but wins on root-mean-square error (0.146 against 0.242), and its root-mean-square error is close to listwise deletion's 0.143.
In the applied illustration it detected the complete-data group difference nearly as often as listwise deletion did (32% against 36% of replications at 40% missing).
We therefore see no efficiency argument for pooling in this setting.
The recommendation has one measured cost.

Under group-asymmetric selection on X (missing not at random), group-wise imputation rejected a true null at 0.073 against a nominal 0.05, 2.8 Monte Carlo standard errors above it, while pooled imputation rejected at 0.004 ( §Results 4a).
Because the failure is one-directional under a statable condition, the reading rule is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the practically useful part.
A study that used default imputation and reported no difference carries little information about whether one exists.
At 40% missing, the procedure removes roughly half the difference on the z scale, and in the applied cases it removed four in five of the detections (UCI) and all of them (iris).
Outside the class in which the groups share slope and residual variance, a null report carries little information at the missing rates studied here.

The attenuation itself, however, is one-directional only within the class we model -standardised groups, a common Y distribution, selection on Y. Outside it the general form permits the completed contrast to be shrunk, exaggerated, reversed or manufactured, which leaves a null report weak for a wider set of reasons rather than for this one.
A study that used default imputation and did report a difference cannot be cleared by inspecting its variances.
The "erase only" reading holds when the null case has a common population conditional slope and residual variance.
That condition is sufficient; it is also necessary, apart from a zero shared slope, only if the reading must hold at every missing rate (two groups, missingness completely at random).

Comparable-looking marginal sample variances do not establish it: two groups with equal nonzero correlations and unequal spread already differ in slope or in residual variance, and sampling error puts the required equality beyond the reach of any eyeball check.
The defensible rule is procedural rather than diagnostic:

A pooled-imputation result should be re-estimated with group-specific slopes and residual variances, or under an explicitly congenial joint model, before the reported difference is treated as established.
Comparable observed variances are at most a weak warning diagnostic, never a guarantee.

If the groups' variances visibly differ, the finding warrants reanalysis with group-specific conditional models rather than outright rejection, and a large study reports the artefact as significant more often than a small one does.
With equal true correlations and a two-fold difference in the spread of the complete variable, pooled imputation manufactures ζ = -0.121 out of nothing.
At a three-fold ratio with 40% missing and N = 640 it declares that difference significant in 31% of analyses ( §Results 4b).
The rejection rate rises with N and tends to 1 in those designs, because each has a fixed nonzero contrast limit.
Unequal variances alone do not produce one: two groups with no association at all keep a zero contrast exactly, at every rate and at any spread ratio ( §Appendix).
The asymmetry we originally claimed, that pooling can erase but never manufacture, is real in the standardised design and not beyond it.

The asymmetry arises because a true null there forces a common X | Y slope and a common residual variance, which is the class pooling leaves untouched, while a real difference forces unequal slopes and is shrunk.
Equal nonzero correlations with unequal spread ratios σ X /σ Y break the first condition.
Equal correlations and equal slopes with unequal spread break the second.
Either breach alone puts the null outside the untouched class and makes the failure run in both directions.
We state the condition prominently because the weaker, unconditional version is the more quotable one, and because it is wrong.
That rule differs from the one governing the companion paper's deterministic regression imputation, which can manufacture an effect under much broader conditions.
Keeping the two straight matters, because the summary "uncongenial imputation is dangerous" is too coarse to act on.
The kind of danger depends on which member of the family the analyst used.
The coverage result is neither a paradox nor new asymptotics.
It is the standard consequence of an inconsistent estimator combined with a shrinking interval, for which Morris, White and Crowther (2019, p. 2087) give the general statement.

text.text: Because the bias is a near-fixed share of the estimand at a given design and roughly constant in N, while the standard error falls at rate 1/√N, the ratio of the two grows without bound, and the interval becomes both narrower and no better centred.
In our grid, coverage at π = 0.40 runs 0.992, 0.974, 0.903 and 0.703 as N goes from 40 to 320, reaching 0.584 on the robustness design.
The practical trap lies in the direction of the error at small N. The pooled arm looks better than nominal when the sample is small, because between-imputation variance inflates its intervals.
A researcher piloting at N = 40 therefore sees conservative intervals, concludes that the method is safe, and scales up into precisely the regime where it fails.
The same structure produces the false positives reported in §Results 4b, and the two are best understood as one phenomenon rather than as two findings.

Applied to a real difference, that growing ratio destroys coverage; applied to a manufactured one, it destroys Type I control, which rises from 0.026 to 0.309 as N goes from 80 to 640 in the worst cell.
Every diagnostic a researcher might use for reassurance, whether more data, tighter intervals, or a significant result, moves in the wrong direction.
The two papers describe the same mechanism with different consequences.

In both, an imputation model omits a term that the analysis model contains, and the estimand attached to that term is attenuated in large samples by an exact factor κ(π) of the same order as the missing fraction -not the same κ in the two papers, and here κ/π runs from 1.40 down to 1.07 across π.
At the 40% both papers headline, ours is 0.457 and the companion's 0.384, either side of 0.400.
The companion's factor crosses below π near 0.32.
Ours never does in our range.

The companion's omitted term is a product X₁X₂, whereas this paper's is group × Y. Both imputation models nonetheless include the outcome, the pooled model drawing X from Y and group, so the distortion studied here is distinct from the better-known failure of omitting the outcome, which biases the covariate-outcome relationship itself under stochastic imputation (D'Agostino McGowan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The companion's omitted term is a product X₁X₂, whereas this paper's is group × Y. Both imputation models nonetheless include the outcome, the pooled model drawing X from Y and group, so the distortion studied here is distinct from the better-known failure of omitting the outcome, which biases the covariate-outcome relationship itself under stochastic imputation (D'Agostino <ref type="bibr">McGowan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Figure 8 puts both papers' attenuation factors on one pair of axes -ours, and the companion's under both MAR and MCAR, three curves in all -which is legitimate because each κ is the same kind of quantity: the dimensionless fraction of a true effect destroyed.
They are not the same curve.

Against the companion's MAR factor, ours agrees to 0.010 for π ≤ 0.10 and separates to 0.087 by π = 0.50, with pooling across groups costing more than omitting an interaction at every rate the figure plots (π from 0.05 to 0.50) at this paper's base design.
Both factors are evaluated by quadrature, so the small-π agreement is a feature of the curves, not a limit on the comparison.
The instructive difference lies in the boundary, and it is narrower than the symmetry suggests.

Deterministic regression imputation manufactures interactions that are not there, switched on in the companion's bivariatenormal design by a single selection moment that alone fixes neither its sign nor its magnitude, and it does so under a wide range of conditions.

Pooled imputation is guaranteed, in large samples, not to manufacture a correlation difference whenever the groups match on both the slope and the residual variance and, within each group, X depends on Y linearly with a residual variance that does not change with Y. Those conditions are sufficient: under them the closed form returns exactly zero for any selection on Y. Under selection on Y, a residual spread that changes with Y or a curved relation can break the guarantee even when the slope and residual variance match ( §Theory, "The general form").

Under selection on Y, the designs in which we have seen it manufacture one are designs where the groups differ in scale; under group-asymmetric selection on X every arm shows a spurious difference, pooling least ( §4a).

The two failures are therefore not opposites: one is broadly prone to false positives, the other conditionally so -and its condition concerns population slopes and residual variances, so unequal observed group variances flag the risk rather than measuring it.
One selection mechanism.
The main grid and the closed form assume missingness at random on the fully observed variable Y, with a logistic tilt of fixed strength.
Selection on Y alone makes E[X | Y, observed] = ρ g •Y hold, and hence makes the closed form clean.

It also means that the specific shape of κ(π), in particular the finding that κ/π declines from 1.40 to 1.07 across π, is a property of this mechanism rather than a universal constant of pooled imputation.
Missingness depending on X itself is now partly covered rather than merely disclaimed ( §Results 4a).
The exact-zero boundary is specific to selection on Y: under group-asymmetric MNAR on X, a difference does appear under the null.

The practical rule nevertheless survives, because the distortion originates in the mechanism rather than in the imputation, with listwise deletion the most displaced arm and pooled imputation the least.
In that setting the pooled arm's Type I error is 0.004, while the congenial group-wise arm reaches 0.073, which is 2.8 Monte Carlo standard errors above nominal.

The congenial arm is the anti-conservative one there because of its own displacement rather than because congeniality reproduces a compromised target: group-wise imputation fitted to X-selected cases has a displaced limit of its own, -0.0369 against listwise's -0.0429.
None of the three procedures models X-dependent selection, so the experiment does not show that no imputation model could.
We have not covered MNAR combined with genuinely different correlations, or missingness driven by an unobserved third variable.
κ depends on the gap and the level, not only on π. κ is not a function of π alone.
It rises with |ρ₁ -ρ₂|, from 0.448 at a gap of 0.10 to 0.539 at a gap of 0.90 with π = 0.40.
At a fixed gap it also moves with where the two correlations sit.

Two pairs sharing a gap of 0.40 at levels 0.40 and 0.50 agree to 0.001, but at a gap of 0.10 κ moves by 0.016 between levels 0 and 0.55, and at a gap of 0.40 it reaches 0.646 when the larger correlation is 0.99 ( §Results 3a).

Over the tabulated pairs with gaps up to 0.4 and mean correlation no more than 0.5, κ varied by under 0.01, but not at higher levels (0.4877 at ρ = (0.90, 0.50) against 0.4567 at (0.60, 0.20), π = 0.40).
Planning should use the full-design κ(π, ρ₁, ρ₂) rather than read κ(π) as a one-argument function.
A level effect of 0.001 is inside the ±0.01 noise floor of a Monte Carlo evaluator, which is how it read as invariance.
At a gap of 0.90 the departure from the main design is eight times that floor.
An invariance claim needs an evaluator finer than the effect it is testing.
Normality.
Within-group bivariate normality is assumed and used twice.
The applied illustrations can neither show nor rule out a normality effect.

The incremental prediction came within 0.010 of the plim on iris (+0.0061 at π = .20, -0.0099 at π = .40) and within 0.007 on the discrete UCI scores at π = .20, and it differed by 0.050 on UCI at π = .40.
All four gaps lie inside the variation that exactly normal data would show.

For a normal dataset with the same group sizes, means, spreads and correlations, the increment (averaged over maskings, so that only the dataset varies) has a standard deviation across such datasets at π = .40 of about 0.06 for iris and 0.1 for UCI, and it exceeds the UCI plim by 0.050 or more about three times in ten (verify/p36_p2g22v_B_spread.py).
Testing the normality assumption needs more datasets, or larger ones.
One test could falsify the closed form.

Take one large public dataset (N ≥ 5,000), or many screened datasets, mask the incomplete variable as here, and compare the pooled-minus-group-wise increment with its plim against a Gaussian null matched to each dataset's moments.
The closed form fails if the increment misses the plim by more than normal data of that size would allow.
The researcher of the Introduction asks whether rumination tracks depressive symptoms more closely in a clinical sample than in controls.
For that researcher the rule is short.
A null from pooled imputation says little either way.

A reported difference may be shrunk or, when the groups differ in the spread of the complete variable, partly manufactured, so it should be re-estimated with imputation inside each group before it is believed.
Result 1 is the general form of "A + B = 1": that statement was the σ² Y = 1 case.
With the pooled model X ~Y + group fitted on the observed cases,

The blend structure is now exact and carries no leftover offset term -the k g of the special case was an artefact of the standardised parameterisation, and it is absorbed into ℬ g by the (c g -a g )² piece.
Observed cases contribute the group's own slope β g , weighted by 𝒜 g ; imputed cases contribute the pooled slope b, weighted by ℬ g.
So b is a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes, weighted by each group's share of the observed sample times the variance of Y among its observed cases.
That is the general statement of which b = (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2 is a corollary: make the groups exchangeable and equally sampled and every weight coincides.
Set w g = ½, μ g = 0, σ Yg = σ Xg = 1 and a common selection rule.
Then β g = ρ g , τ² g = 1 -ρ² g , V o and f are shared, so b = (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2, 𝒜 g + ℬ g = 1, and the expressions collapse to §Steps 3-5.
Checked numerically: the general routine reproduces the special-case value to 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁶ at π = .20 and 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ at π = .40 (R/drv004_general.R).

The general form is verified against simulation step by step on three designs that break every symmetry -unequal shares, means, SDs, correlations and group-specific selection -45 checks, 0 failures (R/verify_drv004_general.R).
The null result now follows from the algebra.

The covariance is exactly right.
The variance is not, unless τ² g = τ² as well.

So the boundary needs two things, and the special case hid the second by making them the same condition: if the groups share both the slope β g and the residual variance τ² g , then Var g (X*) = β²σ² Yg + τ² and a zero contrast stays zero, and so does any contrast, zero or not: plim ζ = ζ, for any selection on Y, group-specific or not.

κ depends on the missing fraction, the gap between the correlations, and their level κ moves mostly with the gap, and at a fixed gap also with the level. κ depends on π alone to within 0.010 across three designs, which is inside the noise floor of the Monte Carlo evaluator.
Evaluated exactly by quadrature, κ moves with the gap between the two correlations.
Two pairs sharing a gap of 0.40 at levels 0.40 and 0.50 agree to within 0.0011, which is how the level came to look irrelevant.
It is not irrelevant: at the same gap κ reaches 0.6462 at (.99, .59), and at a gap of 0.10 it falls by 0.016 between levels 0 and 0.55.
§Results 3a tabulates the designs.

Three things follow from having the closed form that the simulation alone would not give: 2. κ can be read off before collecting data, for any π, from quadrature rather than a new simulation -which is what makes the result usable as a planning quantity.
It says which feature of the design controls the damage.
The attenuation runs through A g , the observed-case share within each group.

We offered that as a prediction rather than a post-hoc account, and §Results 5d has since tested it on iris and rejected it: holding the asymmetric deletion rates almost fixed at 0.267 / 0.532 while equalising the two species' spreads and correlations drops the manufactured displacement from 0.1227 to 0.0001.
So the uneven loss of values accounts for essentially none of the applied illustration's excess over the balanced simulation, and the 1.80-fold spread ratio accounts for it instead.

text.text: A reader of this one should not have to hold another manuscript to check the argument.
Everything above computes completed moments and then forms a correlation from them.
Those moments are governed by three lines that govern every estimand of this kind, and those lines also say precisely where this paper's estimand is different.
Write an analysis as a regression of an outcome on a feature vector Z, and let G = E[ZZ′] and c = E[ZY] be its population moments, so the true coefficients are β = G⁻¹c.
Assume (i) missingness completely at random at rate π, and (ii) an imputation procedure whose limiting conditional law for the filled-in value is fixed as π varies.
Condition (ii) is a real restriction rather than a restatement of (i): missingness completely at random says how rows are chosen, and says nothing about how the software fills them.
This paper's pooled and group-wise imputers satisfy it, because they are fitted to the observed rows, which under (i) follow the population law at every rate.

Under those two conditions a fraction 1π of rows carry the real features and a fraction π carry features built from an imputed value, so G*(π) = (1π)G + πG imp , c*(π) = (1π)c + πc imp , and neither imputed-row moment set depends on π.
Both pooled moments are straight lines in the missing rate.

The bias is then exactly β*β = G*(π)⁻¹(c*(π) -G*(π)β), and differentiating at π = 0 gives the first-order cost as G⁻¹d, where is the moment defect of the imputed rows: how far the filled-in rows fall from satisfying the analysis's own normal equations.
The estimator is exact at every missing rate exactly when d = 0.
That is normalequation compatibility, not a definition of congeniality in Meng's (1994) sense.

Congeniality asks the imputer and the analyst to agree with each other, not with the population, so a shared but misspecified model can leave d ≠ 0; and d = 0 can also arise through cancellation without congeniality.
The condition d = 0 is nonetheless sharper than asking the imputation to preserve the joint distribution, which is sufficient for exactness but stronger than necessary.

With the Gram matrix held fixed, a regression coefficient is linear in the cross-moment vector, so the defect converts to a coefficient error in one matrix multiplication -by G*(π)⁻¹ exactly, and by G⁻¹ at first order in the rate.
Jointly in both moment sets the coefficient is not linear at all: G⁻¹c is scale-invariant, since multiplying G and c by one constant leaves it unchanged.
A correlation admits no such conversion.
It is a ratio, σ XY ⁄ σ X σ Y , and the contrast then applies Fisher's transform on top.

So the law above does not deliver ζ directly; it delivers the moments, and the ratio and the transform are a further step -which is exactly the step Theory Steps 6 and 7 take, from the moments of Result 2 of this appendix, for this design.
Two things follow that are worth stating plainly.
The moments this paper computes are the same objects the general law takes as input, which is why the pooled slope b appears in both accounts as the thing the imputed rows are told to believe.

And the nonlinearity is not a technicality: because a correlation is a ratio, a defect in the covariance and a defect in the variance can partly cancel, which is precisely why the boundary condition above is necessary, for two groups under missingness completely at random, only once the missing rate is allowed to vary, and why a single rate can hide a real difference.

We see the broader contrast though some details stay concealed Pooling can erase a difference or make a false one seem revealed The map is incomplete though the central risk remains More data can strengthen bias while confidence steadily gains

text.text: The special case in the body carries the argument.
This appendix drops every symmetry the design assumes -equal groups, a common Y distribution, identical selection -and shows the same law survives.
It is verification, and it is also where the boundary condition is stated correctly, because the special case makes two distinct conditions look like one.
No real dataset satisfies those three symmetries, and the applied illustration had to be evaluated by a bespoke routine rather than by the formula.
So we give the general result.
It is not much harder, it contains the special case, and -as §Results 4b reports -it overturns a claim we made from the special case alone.
Missingness may depend on Y in a group-specific way: P(missing | Y = y, g) = u g (y), an arbitrary function.
Write f g = P(observed | g), and let a g , V og be the mean and variance of Y among that group's observed cases, c g , V mg the same among its missing cases.
The two quantities that carry everything
In words: 𝒜 g is the observed rows' share of group g's outcome variance; ℬ g is the missing rows' share, together with the shift between the two rows' means.
Sufficient -and necessary, once the missing rate is allowed to vary.

Both completed moments are affine in the observed fraction, so matching the groups at every rate is a set of coefficient equations, not the one scalar equation that made cancellation look unavoidable.
Solved, they force both conditions (proof below): a shared slope alone leaves the variance wrong, a shared residual variance alone the covariance.

Cancellation at a single rate survives: in the recorded example, whose true contrast is 0.086, the two completed correlations coincide at an observed fraction of 3/5 (40% missing) and at no other interior rate, so a real difference vanishes there.
Say what "every rate" buys, because the quantifier carries the whole claim and costs nothing to state.

For two groups under missingness completely at random at a fraction common to both, with any positive group shares, any positive outcome variances -equal or not -and positive residual variances, the completed Fisher-z contrast equals the true contrast at every observed fraction if and only if the groups share the slope, and share the residual variance unless that shared slope is zero.
The zero-slope case is the trivial exception: with no association in either group both completed correlations are zero at every rate whatever the residual variances are.

Necessity is proved here on the completely-at-random sub-family, which is the stronger reading rather than a weaker one -fewer mechanisms are needed to pin the two conditions down, and sufficiency above still holds for any selection on Y and any number of groups.
Proof of necessity, checkable by hand.

Take two groups with shares w₁, w₂ > 0, outcome variances σ² Y1 , σ² Y2 > 0, slopes β g and residual variances τ² g > 0, and missingness completely at random at a fraction π common to both, so the observed fraction is f = 1π.
text.formatted: Take two groups with shares w₁, w₂ > 0, outcome variances σ² Y1 , σ² Y2 > 0, slopes β g and residual variances τ² g > 0, and missingness completely at random at a fraction π common to both, so the observed fraction is f = 1π.

text.text: Result 2 then gives each group's completed correlation as an affine numerator over the square root of a positive affine variance:
At f = 1 these are the true correlations.
Suppose atanh r₁ -atanh r₂ equals the true contrast ζ at every f in (0, 1].
Both sides are continuous, so the identity also holds at the formal endpoint f = 0, which the proof uses and no study can reach.
Case A, ζ ≠ 0.
Put K = tanh ζ, so 0 < |K| < 1.
text.formatted: Put K = tanh ζ, so 0 < |K| < 1.

text.text: The subtraction formula for tanh turns the identity into r₁ -r₂ = K(1 -r₁r₂), and squaring gives 2(1 -K²)•r₁r₂ = r₁² + r₂² -K²(1 + r₁²r₂²).
Each r² g = A² g /L g is a rational function of f, so r₁r₂ is rational too.
Neither A g vanishes identically, since that would force both slopes to zero and so ζ = 0.
Hence √(L₁L₂) = A₁A₂/(r₁r₂) is rational.
A product of two positive affine functions is the square of a rational function only if both are constant or the two are proportional.
If they are proportional and not constant, r₁ -r₂ is an affine function divided by √L₂, which is rational only when that affine function is zero.
Then r₁ = r₂, so K(1 -r²₁) = 0, which is impossible.
Both L g are therefore constant, and each r g (f) = a g + d g •f is affine.
In r₁ -r₂ = K(1 -r₁r₂) the f² coefficient gives K•d₁d₂ = 0.
If d₁ = 0, the f coefficient gives d₂(1 -K•a₁) = 0, and |K•a₁| < 1 forces d₂ = 0 (the case d₂ = 0 is symmetric).
text.formatted: If d₁ = 0, the f coefficient gives d₂(1 -K•a₁) = 0, and |K•a₁| < 1 forces d₂ = 0 (the case d₂ = 0 is symmetric).

text.text: Each completed correlation is thus constant in the rate.
A constant A g needs β g = b, and a constant L g then needs τ² g = s².
Both groups share the slope and the residual variance.
Case B, ζ = 0 with a common correlation ρ ≠ 0.
Both slopes carry the sign of ρ, so b ≠ 0.
At f = 0, r g = b•σ Yg / √(b²•σ² Yg + s²), which is strictly monotone in σ² Yg , so equality forces σ² Y1 = σ² Y2 .
Write x = β₁, y = β₂, q = w₁ and M = q•x² + (1 -q)•y².
Equal correlations then make each L g a common multiple of M + f(β² g -M), and the two completed correlations share a sign, so equality means equal squares:
The coefficient of f³ in P is q(q -1)(x -y)³(x + y).
With 0 < q < 1 and x, y of the same nonzero sign, it vanishes only when x = y.
text.formatted: With 0 < q < 1 and x, y of the same nonzero sign, it vanishes only when x = y.

text.text: Equal correlations with equal slopes and equal outcome variances then force equal residual variances.
Case C, both correlations zero.
Both slopes are zero, so b = 0, and both completed correlations are zero at every rate whatever the residual variances: the exception.
Sufficiency was shown above, which completes the proof.
It needs no computer algebra.
Each algebraic step is re-derived symbolically by verify/p36_verify_p2_necessity_handproof_2026-11-04.py, with a control beside each check that fails when that step is altered.

The same proof gives something sharper than the contrast statement, and that sharper version is the one to state: under either admitted case each group's completed correlation is individually constant in the rate and equal to its true value.
The contrast is not preserved by two errors cancelling.
So pooled imputation cannot trade one group's distortion against the other's across a range of rates.
At an isolated rate the two distortions can still meet, which is what the 3/5 example shows: there a real difference of 0.086 is completely hidden.
Nothing in a real study tunes the missing rate to a point.
One limitation, and it is about detectability rather than about the algebra.
Necessity here is exact equality, and designs that break both conditions can still preserve the contrast at every rate to within a margin no study of realistic size could resolve.
So the boundary separates designs cleanly in the limit and not at all in practice near its edge.
A reanalysis that finds a stable contrast across missing rates has shown only a small displacement over the rates it examined.
It has not shown that the slopes and residual variances are nearly equal, because weak associations can hold the contrast almost constant while both differ by a fixed amount.

The symbolic certificate verify/p36_verify_p2_unequal_variance_necessity_2026-09-16.wls is a second, independent route to the proof above: it solves the coefficient equations and admits only the same two cases.
R/verify_p2_uniform_necessity.R carries the zero-slope exception and a sweep of 400 random designs that break the conditions, none of which preserves the contrast at every rate to within 10⁻⁹.
It is numerical evidence that fails to contradict the proof rather than the proof, and its verdict line says so.
Both are deposited.
Under the standardised design, ρ₁ = ρ₂ implies β₁ = β₂ and τ²₁ = τ²₂, which is why the boundary looked like a statement about equal correlations.
It is not.

Equal nonzero correlations with unequal ratios σ X /σ Y give unequal slopes, and pooled imputation can then manufacture a difference -see §Results 4b, where ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40 and a two-fold difference in σ Y produces a plim of ζ = -0.121.
The general form above drops all three of the body's symmetries -equal groups, Y standard normal in both, identical selection.

The identity becomes 𝒜 g + ℬ g = Var(Y | g), the pooled slope becomes a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes, and the boundary is restated in the form the algebra supportsa shared slope β g and a shared residual variance τ² g are together sufficient for every contrast, zero or not, to be preserved, for any selection on Y. For two groups under missingness completely at random at a fraction common to both, they are also necessary for preservation at every rate, apart from the trivial case in which neither group has any association.

That correction matters in the body, not only in the appendix: the special case makes those two conditions look like one, which is how we came to state the boundary as a claim about equal correlations.
§Results 4b reports what happens when they come apart.
The general form is verified against simulation on three designs that break every symmetry -45 checks, 0 failures (R/verify_drv004_general.R).
The closed form is evaluated by quadrature, not by Monte Carlo.

Every moment in the derivation ( §Theory) is a one-dimensional integral of a normal density against a logistic weight; estimating them by simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶ leaves roughly ±0.01 of noise on κ, which is the same size as some of the effects below and would make them undetectable. zeta_plim_exact() in R/drv004_closedform.R integrates them directly and reproduces all four independently verified designs.

Coverage falls as the sample grows (Figure2, lower row).
At 40% missing it goes from 0.992 at N = 40 to 0.703 at N = 320: a nominal 95% interval covers the truth barely seven times in ten, and the larger study is the one misled.
In the figure only the pooled arm leaves the nominal line, and it does not return to it.
The mechanism is arithmetic rather than subtle -the bias is fixed while the interval narrows at rate 1/√N, so the ratio of bias to standard error grows without bound.

That inversion is the point: more data makes the inference worse, and nothing signals it, because the pooled arm's intervals are if anything wider than nominal at small N (0.992 coverage at N = 40 looks reassuring).
The robustness design reproduces the collapse more strongly: coverage 0.984 → 0.584 (π = 0.40, N = 40 → 320), and 0.989 → 0.862 at π = 0.20.
Power.
The same distortion costs detections.

At π = 0.40, N = 320 the pooled arm rejects ζ = 0 in 0.482 of replications against group-wise imputation's 0.897 -the default imputation model halves the power to find a real difference (results/sequel_grid.csv, power).3.
The attenuation is a law, and we can write it downSources: §Theory; R/verify_conj011.
R; R/drv004_closedform.R; results/sequel_kappa_curve_cf.csv.
Because missingness depends on Y alone, E[X | Y, observed] = ρ g •Y survives selection.

Writing A = P(R = 1)•E[Y² | R = 1] for the observed-case share of the second moment and B = P(R = 0)•E[Y² | R = 0] for the missing-case share, the completed within-group covariance is a blend Cov g (X*, Y) = ρ g •A + b•B + k g •P(R=0)•E[Y | R=0], with b = (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 the pooled slope and k + B = E[Y²] = 1 within each group, regardless of that group's selection.
The weight A is the leading behaviour, not the exact law.

Collecting the offset term with the first gives the exact difference, Cov₁(X*, Y) -Cov₂(X*, Y) = (ρ₁ -ρ₂)•P(R = 1)•Var(Y | R = 1), whose weight is the observed cases' share of the variance of Y: 0.544 at 40% missing, against A = 0.582 ( §Theory, Step 5).
A correlation also needs each group's completed variance of X, and the contrast then passes through Fisher's transform.
The attenuation therefore follows ζ → (1κ)•ζ with κ = κ(π, ρ₁, ρ₂), computed from those moments rather than read off the weight.
Verified against brute-force simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶ across four designs, agreement ≤ 0.002: design ζ plim ζ (closed form) simulation κ ρ = (.6,.
No departure reaches 1.6 Monte Carlo standard errors.

The departures take both signs across the rates, and at π = 0.10 the two sample sizes miss in opposite directions (+0.012 at N = 160, -0.013 at N = 320), so none of them is systematic: the points scatter around the closed form by about what 500 replications allow.κ moves with the gap and, at a fixed gap, with the level.
Over the pairs tabulated below with gaps up to 0.4 and mean correlation no more than 0.5, κ varied by under 0.01.
That does not hold at higher levels: at π = 0.40, κ = 0.4877 for ρ = (0.90, 0.50) against 0.4567 for (0.60, 0.20).
Planning should therefore use the full-design κ(π, ρ₁, ρ₂) rather than read κ off the curve from π alone.
The Appendix gives the quadrature that computes it.
Evaluated exactly, at π = 0.40: which this design standardises to 1 ( §Theory, "The general form").
And k g vanishes because the groups share a slope β g = ρ g •σ Xg /σ Yg -which equal correlations give here only because the variances are equal too.§4b  shows what happens when they are not.

Under the Appendix's model (X linear in Y, residual variance constant in Y) the closed form returns plim ζ = 0 exactly for any selection on Y, and we evaluated it at selection strengths γ Y ∈ {0, 0.7, 1.5}, γ Y being the coefficient on Y in the missingness model ( §Method), including designs in which one group is MAR-on-Y and the other MCAR at the same rate.

Simulation agrees: the probability limit sits at +0.002, and Type I error stays at nominal for the group-wise arm while the pooled arm's stays near zero, with at most one rejection in 300 at each N (Monte Carlo SEs √(p(1 -p)/300) in parentheses): N MI-pooled Type I MI-group-wise Type

Equal correlations, equal slopes, and pooled imputation still manufactures a difference of -0.119 -comparable to the -0.121 produced by unequal slopes.
A rule stated as "safe when the groups share a slope" would pass this design and be wrong on it.
The condition has to name both quantities, which is what §Theory's Result 3 gives.

The null is settled exactly rather than estimated.
With ρ₁ = ρ₂ we get b = ρ, hence k g = 0 and Cov g = ρ(A g + B g ) = ρ for any selection on Y whatsoever -including selection that differs arbitrarily between the groups.
The restriction to selection on Y is not decoration: Step 1 needs it, and §Results 4a shows what happens without it.
That exact null is a proof that pooled imputation cannot manufacture a difference in this standardised design, where equal correlations give equal slopes and equal residual variances.

A simulation could only ever fail to find one.The same algebra gives more than the null, and the general version is worth stating. k g = 0 requires a shared conditional slope, and leaving the completed variance alone requires a shared residual variance.
Neither requirement needs ρ₁ = ρ₂ or equal outcome variances.
Suppose β g ≡ β and τ² g ≡ τ².

Then the pooled imputer recovers exactly those values, b = β and s² = τ², and the completed momentswithin group g are Cov g (X*, Y) = β•Var(Y | g) and Var g (X*) = β²•Var(Y | g) + τ² -thegroup's own population moments, with the missing rate absent from both.

So each correlation is preserved exactly, and so is any contrast between them, zero or not, at every rate and under any admitted selection on Y. Unequal outcome variances are permitted and then the preserved contrast is nonzero: at β = 0.8, τ² = 0.5 and Var(Y | g) = 1 against 4, the true ζ = -0.584 comes back unchanged at every rate (closed form and simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶, with controls that fire when either equality is broken: verify/p36_verify_p2_exact_recovery_2026-10-02.

Within this class pooled imputation does not shrink a real difference either, so the asymmetry of §Discussion is a property of the standardised design -where a null forces the class and a real difference leaves it -and not of the class itself.
